newsitem.title: THAILAND: FOCUS - Thai zero-coupon bonds impact seen limited.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Thai zero-coupon bonds impact seen limited.

text.p: Thailand's issue of 50 billion baht of zero coupon bonds may prevent the immediate collapse of the financial and property sectors but its impact will be limited, analysts said on Tuesday.
The scheme could fall short because of the magnitude of the two sectors' problems -- especially the high degree of financial institution exposure to the oversupply in the property sector, they said.

The cabinet on Tuesday approved the zero coupon bond issue to raise funds to help the two troubled sectors. The government has said the total size of the bond issue could rise to 100 billion baht ($3.85 billion) in future.

The seven-year bond issue is part of a rescue scheme launched by authorities to bail out the financial sector whose rising non-performing loans are mostly due to an over-exposure to the depressed property sector.

Private analysts estimate that the outstanding loans extended to the property sector by commercial banks and finance firms amount to around 800 billion baht, of which anywhere between 20-50 percent could be non-performing loans.
The first tranche of bonds will be auctioned on Friday.

"I think it is the most sensible thing the government could do. I agree that demand side has not been addressed. But there is not much you can do on that now," said Vikas Kawatra, a property analyst at Asia Equity.

"You have a situation where a total number of houses available in the market is close to the number of households in Bangkok...By issuing the zero-coupon bond, you are avoiding the immediate collapse of the financial system," he told Reuters.

Proceeds from the zero-coupon bond auction will be managed by the recently-established government-run Property Loans Management Organization (PMLO) to purchase non-performing property loans from banks and financial companies.
Analysts said the scheme could at least help financial institutions window-dress their balance sheets, which could otherwise be riddled with huge non-performing loans.

"It is absolutely necessary...the government is commendable on that. But one should not expect a miracle from the scheme. It is just a short-term measure..," said an analyst at a U.S. investment bank.
Slowing demand would make a glut in the property sector a problem for some time, analysts said.
Bangkok's office space was likely to incur a vacancy rate of 32 percent by 1998 and residential oversupply was forecast to peak in 1997 at 180,000 units, they said.
There are also problems associated with the bond issue which need to be ironed out.
Analysts questioned whether the nine percent yield attached to the bonds would be attractive enough to lure buyers.
The scheme could force finance companies to sell their assets at significant losses, said Graeme Blench of ABN-AMRO Hoare Govett.

To make profit, the PLMO would need to buy the loans at prices well below the value of assets backing the loans. Writing off these loans could force some finance companies into making further rights issues, he added.
The zero-coupon bond scheme could inadvertently provide funds to financial institutions to continue risky lending practices, Blench said.
